extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), OED staff, and administrative adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (including default judgment consequences, statutory/regulatory bases for misconduct, burden of proof, factors for deciding sanctions, aggravating/mitigating factors, and reinstatement rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural framework and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary hearings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11 (subpart C) and 5 U.S.C. § 556 by a hearing officer appointed by the USPTO; the OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites precedent explaining that 'clear and convincing evidence' is a standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt, requiring evidence that produces a firm belief or conviction. 'Clear' means certain and unambiguous; 'convincing' means reasonable and persuasive. Respondent must receive notice and opportunity for hearing (35 U.S.C. § 32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to answer the Complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent fails to answer, the OED Director may move for default judgment and the court may vacate hearing dates and enter judgment based on the admitted allegations; precedents (e.g., In re Riley) support granting default motions where answers are not filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: criminal act reflecting adversely (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to commit a criminal act that reflects adversely on the practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a practitioner in other respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A felony conviction for conduct such as failure to report or money laundering has been treated as grounds for exclusion; examples and prior exclusions (In re Glazer, In re Caracappa, In re Ho) are cited to show such criminal acts support exclusion from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct: other conduct reflecting adversely (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision can be applied where conduct, even if not directly tied to client matters, undermines fitness to practice (the decision applies it to Respondent's felony conviction involving smuggling/cash evasion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'serious crime' and interim suspension (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.25(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'serious crime' is defined as any criminal offense classified as a felony under U.S., state, or foreign law where it occurred; a practitioner convicted of a serious crime shall receive an interim suspension from practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal felony classifications (e.g., Class D felony definitions) are used to determine seriousness; conviction for a felony is treated as evidence of serious criminal conduct that can lead to exclusion (citations to case law provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of legal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of legal discipline is to protect the public and the administration of justice, not to punish the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary decisions focus on protecting clients, the public, the legal system, and maintaining integrity of the profession (citing ABA STANDARDS and case law). This normative purpose guides sanction selection (e.g., exclusion vs. suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four factors for determining appropriate disciplinary sanction (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining discipline the court considers: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, and/or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors and cites STANDARDS § 3.0; the factors are evaluated together to select an appropriate sanction (with examples from prior USPTO decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty owed to clients, the public, and the legal system (integrity requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental duty of a lawyer is to maintain standards of personal integrity; lawyers must be honest and abide by the law because public confidence depends on officers of the court being above reproach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of this duty (e.g., illegal or dishonest conduct) undermine public confidence and can warrant severe sanctions including disbarment/exclusion; case citations illustrate that false swearing, fraud, or other serious criminal conduct violate this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state evaluation: intentional, knowing, negligent
rubrics_metrics.description: The lawyer's mental state at the time of misconduct (intentional, knowing, or negligent) is decisive in determining culpability; intentional or knowing conduct is sanctioned more severely than negligent conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional conduct involves a conscious objective or purpose to accomplish a result; examples and precedents (STANDARDS § 3.0, case law) show higher culpability and harsher discipline for deliberate misconduct. The decision finds Respondent acted intentionally and knowingly in attempting to evade reporting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of actual or potential injury (harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment includes the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; actual harm is not required—potential harm suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary systems protect the public and deter misconduct; courts have held that even absent client harm, misconduct that poses potential harm or undermines integrity justifies sanction (citing In re Fuess and other authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors are considerations that justify increasing the degree of discipline; the STANDARDS list eleven such factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples present in this case include (i) dishonest or selfish motive (Standard § 9.22(b)) and (ii) substantial experience in the practice of law (Standard § 9.22(i)). Prior decisions illustrate that these aggravating factors support exclusion or more severe discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA STANDARDS § 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors are considerations that may justify reducing the degree of discipline; the STANDARDS list several mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only mitigating factor identified here is absence of a prior disciplinary record (Standard § 9.32(a)). The decision explains that the respondent's clean record was outweighed by the gravity of the violation and aggravating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of ABA STANDARDS and precedent in sanction selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO references and uses the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and prior disciplinary decisions and opinions (including state bar decisions) to inform appropriate sanctions under the USPTO Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision cites multiple prior USPTO disciplinary matters and ABA commentary as persuasive authority when determining sanctions and interpreting aggravating/mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations during suspension/exclusion and reinstatement eligibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner must comply with the responsibilities in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58; an excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of the exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b)), subject to full compliance with § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision orders exclusion nunc pro tunc to a specified date and directs the respondent to refer to the cited regulations for duties and steps required for reinstatement eligibility.
